questions.q: Why would Castlebridge Logistics use the HTTP action to reach Meridian TrackAPI instead of a dedicated Power Automate connector?
options: The HTTP action is faster for every call regardless of the target system
No Power Automate connector exists for Meridian TrackAPI, so the HTTP action calls its REST endpoint directly
Connectors cannot send GET requests, only HTTP actions can
The HTTP action is required before any connector can be used in the same flow
questions.explain: A connector is a pre-built wrapper around an API. When no connector exists for a system, the HTTP action lets the flow call its REST endpoint directly instead.

questions.q: Which part of an HTTP action determines whether the call is reading, creating, updating, or deleting data?
options: The headers
The URI
The method
The body
questions.explain: The method (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) determines what kind of operation the call performs.

questions.q: A flow calls Meridian TrackAPI and the response comes back with a 404 status code. What does that most likely mean?
options: The request succeeded and returned data
The server had an internal error unrelated to the request
The URI or shipment ID in the request doesn't exist
The flow was not authenticated
questions.explain: A 404 means the requested resource — in this case, the URI or shipment ID — wasn't found. 401/403 would indicate an authentication problem, and 5xx would indicate a server-side error.

questions.q: Why would a GET request to Meridian's shipment status endpoint typically have no body?
options: GET requests are not allowed to include headers
A GET is only asking to read data, so there's nothing to send — a body is more commonly used with POST or PUT
Bodies are only supported in Power Automate connectors, not HTTP actions
The body is automatically generated from the URI
questions.explain: GET requests read data and don't need to send a payload. POST and PUT typically include a body because they create or update something.

questions.q: What is the best practice after an HTTP action that might fail, such as a call to an external carrier API?
options: Assume the call succeeded and continue the flow unconditionally
Check the returned status code with a condition and branch to a retry, alert, or logging path on failure
Delete the flow and rebuild it
Remove the headers so the call can't fail
questions.explain: Checking the status code and branching on it (via a Condition or a Run After setting) lets the flow handle failures gracefully instead of breaking silently.
